learn.title: Green Bonds and Climate Finance
learn.intro: Green bonds are debt instruments that fund renewable energy, efficiency, and clean transport projects. They channel trillions from institutional investors toward climate solutions, making them essential financial engines for the global energy transition away from fossil fuels.
learn.c1_text: Green bonds work like regular bonds but proceeds must fund environmental projects. Like a labeled savings jar, investors know their money specifically supports solar farms or wind parks. In 2021, global green bond issuance reached $517 billion, with energy buildings being the largest use category.
learn.c2_text: Renewable energy projects require massive upfront capital—often hundreds of millions for utility-scale solar. Green bonds let developers borrow from pension funds, insurance companies, and sovereign wealth funds, lowering financing costs by 20-100 basis points compared to conventional loans.
learn.c3_text: India issued its first sovereign green bonds in January 2023, raising $1 billion to fund solar, wind, and clean transport. SEBI's Green Debt Security framework mandates that 75% of proceeds finance eligible green projects, accelerating capital toward India's 500 GW non-fossil target by 2030.
learn.stat1: Global cumulative green bond issuance: $2.5 trillion (2014-2022)
learn.stat2: India sovereign green bond first tranche: $1 billion (Jan 2023)
learn.stat3: Green bond growth rate: 50% annually in early 2020s
learn.stat4: Renewable energy share of green bond use of proceeds: 32%

learn.title: Sodium-Ion Batteries Explained
learn.intro: Sodium-ion batteries are emerging as a cheaper, more sustainable alternative to lithium-ion chemistry. Using abundant salt instead of scarce lithium, they promise to democratize energy storage for grid-scale applications, especially in countries like India with limited lithium reserves.
learn.c1_text: Both batteries shuttle ions between electrodes during charge cycles. Sodium ions are larger than lithium ions, giving sodium batteries slightly lower energy density (100-160 Wh/kg vs 150-250 Wh/kg) but unlimited raw material supply. Sodium is 1,000 times more abundant than lithium in Earth's crust.
learn.c2_text: Sodium-ion cells excel in cold weather, maintaining 90% capacity at -20°C where lithium-ion struggles. They have longer cycle life (3,000-6,000 cycles) and zero thermal runaway risk, making them ideal for stationary grid storage, though currently bulkier per kWh than lithium iron phosphate batteries.
learn.c3_text: India imports nearly all its lithium needs but has vast domestic sodium reserves from salt flats in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu. ISRO, Reliance, and local startups are piloting sodium-ion production. The technology supports India's Atmanirbhar Bharat vision by reducing critical mineral import dependence for storage.
learn.stat1: Sodium abundance: 2.6% of Earth's crust vs lithium at 0.002%
learn.stat3: Energy density range: 100-160 Wh/kg for sodium-ion
learn.stat4: Cycle life potential: up to 6,000 cycles for sodium-ion cells

learn.title: Building Integrated Photovoltaics BIPV
learn.intro: Building Integrated Photovoltaics (BIPV) transform buildings into power generators by replacing conventional materials like roof tiles, windows, and facades with solar cells. They slash urban energy use while eliminating the land footprint of solar farms.
learn.c1_text: BIPV replaces building components rather than mounting panels on top. Think of solar roof shingles, semi-transparent windows, and ventilated facades. They serve dual purposes—weatherproofing and electricity generation—cutting material costs while generating 20-50 W per square foot of surface.
learn.c2_text: Modern BIPV products offer customizable colors, transparency levels, and textures. Thin-film technologies like CIGS and amorphous silicon enable curved surfaces and building contours. Unlike rack-mounted panels, BIPV systems require no additional mounting hardware, reducing installation labor by 30-40%.
learn.c3_text: India's ECBC+ (Energy Conservation Building Code) and net-zero building policies promote BIPV adoption. MNRE's PM-Surya Ghar scheme includes BIPV components for new urban construction. Bengaluru and Mumbai developers now market 'solar homes' with integrated roof tiles generating 3-5 kW per household.
learn.stat1: Global BIPV market size: projected $87 billion by 2030
learn.stat2: BIPV efficiency range: 10-22% depending on technology
learn.stat3: Building sector global energy use: 30% of total consumption
learn.stat4: Space savings: BIPV eliminates separate solar mounting footprint entirely

learn.title: Solar Panel Types Compared
learn.intro: Not all solar panels are equal. Monocrystalline, polycrystalline, and thin-film technologies differ in efficiency, cost, appearance, and ideal applications. Understanding these differences helps homeowners, businesses, and utilities choose the right panel for their specific needs and climate.
learn.c1_text: Monocrystalline panels are made from a single silicon crystal, giving them a uniform black appearance. They offer the highest efficiency at 20-25%, performing better in limited space. Premium residential installations favor mono panels despite their 10-15% higher cost per watt compared to alternatives.
learn.c2_text: Polycrystalline panels are made by melting multiple silicon fragments together, creating a speckled blue look. They are cheaper to produce, with efficiency between 15-20%. They need more roof area for the same power output and perform slightly worse in high temperatures, losing about 0.5% efficiency per °C above 25°C.
learn.c3_text: Thin-film panels use non-crystalline silicon or alternative materials like CdTe and CIGS deposited on glass, plastic, or metal. They are 90% lighter, work in low light, and are flexible. Indian solar farms often use First Solar's CdTe thin-film because of superior performance in hot, dusty conditions at 16-18% efficiency.
learn.stat1: Monocrystalline efficiency record: 26.1% in lab conditions
learn.stat3: Thin-film cost advantage: 20-30% cheaper than crystalline
learn.stat4: Global solar PV market share by technology: mono dominates at 80%+

learn.title: Small Wind Turbines for Homes
learn.intro: Small wind turbines—typically rated between 400 watts and 100 kW—let homes, farms, and communities generate their own electricity. Unlike utility-scale wind farms, they can be installed on-site with minimal permitting, offering energy independence in rural and off-grid locations.
learn.c1_text: Small wind turbines use lift and drag forces from wind hitting angled blades. As blades spin, they turn a shaft connected to a generator, producing electricity. Cut-in speeds are typically 6-9 mph, and most produce rated power at 25-30 mph. A 10 kW system can power a small home.
learn.c2_text: Turbine tower height should be at least 30 feet above any obstacle within 300 feet. Annual wind speed of 10+ mph is essential—a 1 mph increase can boost energy output by 20-30%. Most systems use 3 blades for smoother operation and lower noise than 2-blade designs.
learn.c3_text: India's distributed wind program supports small turbines in rural areas where grid supply is unreliable. Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, and Karnataka host hundreds of small wind installations. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy offers subsidies of ₹50,000-₹1.5 lakh per unit, depending on capacity.
learn.stat1: Global small wind capacity: over 1.3 GW installed
learn.stat2: Small wind market size: 250,000+ units shipped annually
learn.stat3: India's small wind subsidy: up to ₹1.5 lakh per unit
learn.stat4: Typical home turbine: 1.5-10 kW generating 3,000-25,000 kWh yearly

learn.title: Wave Energy Converters Explained
learn.intro: Wave energy converters harvest the powerful, consistent motion of ocean waves to generate clean electricity. With global wave energy potential estimated at 29,500 TWh per year, this emerging technology could power the world many times over, especially in coastal nations like India.
learn.c1_text: Wave energy converters fall into three categories: point absorbers (buoy floating on surface), attenuators (long segments parallel to wave direction), and oscillating water columns (air trapped in chambers). Each exploits different wave physics, with point absorbers like the Swedish CorPower system producing 600 kW per unit.
learn.c2_text: Waves carry kinetic and potential energy in slow, oscillating motions. Power take-off systems convert these gentle movements into electricity using hydraulic rams, direct-drive linear generators, or air turbines. The challenge is surviving 50-foot storm waves while capturing energy from 2-foot everyday swells.
learn.c3_text: India's 7,500 km coastline receives consistent monsoonal waves averaging 1.5-2.5 meters. The Ministry of Earth Sciences and IIT Madras have tested prototypes near Vizhinjam and Andaman Islands. India's National Institute of Ocean Technology estimates 40 GW of recoverable wave energy along Tamil Nadu and Kerala coasts.
learn.stat1: Global wave energy potential: 29,500 TWh annually
learn.stat2: Wave energy density: 30-70 kW per meter of wavefront
learn.stat3: CorPower system output: 600 kW per commercial unit
learn.stat4: India's estimated wave energy potential: 40 GW along southern coast
